question: Where do I hire a fractional CRO?
body:
## Direct Answer
You hire a fractional CRO through four main channels: specialized fractional-executive marketplaces (Chief Outsiders, Go Fractional, Continuum, Bolster), boutique RevOps and GTM advisory firms, warm referrals from your investors and peer founders, and direct outreach on LinkedIn to operators who list "fractional" or "advisor" in their headline. For most Seed-to-Series-B companies, referrals and a targeted marketplace search close the strongest candidates fastest, because the role is trust-dense and the best fractional CROs are rarely actively job-hunting.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior go-to-market leader who runs your revenue engine part-time — typically one to three days a week — instead of joining as a full-time hire. Companies reach for one when revenue has outgrown founder-led selling but can't yet justify a $300K+ base plus equity for a full-time CRO. The hard part isn't deciding you need one; it's knowing *where* the credible ones actually live, how to filter operators from coaches, and how to structure the engagement so you get an accountable revenue owner rather than an expensive strategy deck. This essay maps every sourcing channel, the vetting bar, and the mechanics of a first engagement.

## What channels actually surface qualified fractional CROs?

There are five sourcing channels, and they are not equal in signal quality. **Warm referrals** are the highest-conversion path: ask your lead investor, your board, and two or three founders who are one stage ahead of you who fixed *their* revenue motion. Investors in particular keep informal benches of fractional operators they've seen perform inside portfolio companies, and a partner-level intro moves a strong candidate to a call within days. The referral also carries embedded due diligence — someone you trust has already watched this person operate under pressure.

The reason referrals convert so well is structural, not just social. A fractional CRO is being handed the keys to your revenue — your forecast, your pipeline data, your comp plan, and often your most senior sellers. That is a trust-dense transaction, and trust does not transfer through a résumé. When a founder you respect says "this person took us from flat to predictable in a quarter," they are compressing months of observation into a single sentence that no interview can replicate. The practical move is to make your ask specific: don't email your investor "know any fractional CROs?" — ask "who fixed the revenue motion at a company selling roughly what we sell, at roughly our stage, in the last two years?" Specific asks produce specific names; vague asks produce a list of everyone's second cousin who "does sales stuff."

![Where do I hire a fractional CRO — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9202-b1.jpg)


**Fractional-executive marketplaces** are the highest-volume path. Platforms such as Go Fractional, Continuum, Bolster (co-founded by former Return Path CEO Matt Blumberg), Chief Outsiders, and Graham Weaver-adjacent operator networks curate vetted senior GTM leaders and let you filter by industry, motion (PLG vs. sales-led), and stage. Bolster in particular was built around board-and-executive matching and skews toward operators who have carried a real revenue number. The tradeoff versus referrals is that you do more of the vetting yourself, because the platform verifies background but not fit.

The remaining three channels are **boutique advisory firms** (RevOps and GTM shops that will staff a fractional CRO out of their partner bench), **direct LinkedIn outreach** (search "Fractional CRO," "Fractional VP Sales," or "GTM Advisor" and filter by people who scaled a company through your exact stage), and **operator communities** like Pavilion, RevGenius, and Operators Guild, where fractional leaders are members and word-of-mouth is native. Each of these has a distinct grain. Boutique firms give you continuity and a bench — if your first operator isn't the right fit, the firm re-staffs rather than leaving you to restart the search — but you sometimes pay a firm markup and get an operator who is one of several accounts on their plate. LinkedIn outreach is the most controllable and the most laborious: you own the filtering entirely, which is powerful when you know exactly the motion and vertical you need, and exhausting when you don't. Communities sit in between — the vetting is social rather than contractual, and the quality of a Pavilion or Operators Guild lead depends heavily on how active and specific you are inside the community. The diagram below shows how these channels feed a single pipeline.

![Where do I hire a fractional CRO — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9202-b2.jpg)


```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Need a fractional CRO] --> B[Warm referrals from investors and founders]
    A --> C[Fractional marketplaces]
    A --> D[Boutique GTM advisory firms]
    A --> E[LinkedIn direct outreach]
    A --> F[Operator communities]
    B --> G[Candidate shortlist]
    C --> G
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Vet for operator versus coach]
    H --> I[Paid trial engagement]
    I --> J[Ongoing fractional CRO]
```

A practical sequence: fire off referral asks first because they take days to bear fruit, then run a marketplace search in parallel so you have volume, and use LinkedIn and communities to fill gaps in specific expertise (a PLG motion, a vertical, a channel you're weak in). The mistake founders make is running these channels sequentially — exhausting referrals, then trying marketplaces, then finally posting to a community — which stretches a two-week search into two months while your revenue problem compounds. Run them concurrently and let the channels compete; the strongest candidate often surfaces from the channel you expected least. For a deeper breakdown of how the role differs from a full-time hire, see the framing at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vs-full-time.

![Where do I hire a fractional CRO — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9202-b3.jpg)


## How do I tell a real operator from a "strategy" coach?

This is where most searches go wrong. The title "fractional CRO" is unregulated, and the market is crowded with people who will happily charge $8K–$15K a month to review your funnel and hand you frameworks. A framework is not a revenue engine. The single sharpest filter is **carried quota**: has this person personally owned a number — a real annual quota or a revenue P&L — and hit it, more than once, at a company roughly your size and motion? An operator talks in specifics (ramp times, quota attainment percentages, pipeline coverage ratios, the exact comp plan they rebuilt); a coach talks in principles.

Ask three questions that coaches struggle to answer concretely. First: "Walk me through the last comp plan you designed and what it changed." A real CRO will describe accelerators, clawbacks, and the behavior shift they engineered. Second: "What's your pipeline-coverage target for our stage and why?" — you want a number and a rationale, not "it depends." Third: "What would you do in your first 30 days, and what would you *not* touch?" The restraint half of that answer separates operators who respect existing motion from consultants who rip everything out to justify their fee.

There is a second-order tell worth listening for: how the candidate talks about *failure*. A genuine operator has lost deals, blown a quarter, hired the wrong VP, and shipped a comp plan that backfired — and they'll tell you the story, what it cost, and what they changed. Someone whose career narrative is an unbroken string of wins has either never truly owned the number or is selling you a highlight reel. Ask directly: "Tell me about a revenue plan you built that didn't work, and what you learned." Coaches deflect this into abstractions ("alignment is always the real issue"); operators get specific and slightly uncomfortable, because they lived it.

Reference the outcomes, not the logos. Anyone can list impressive company names on a slide; you need to know what *they specifically* owned there. Was this person the VP Sales who built the AE team from four to twenty and lifted attainment, or were they a senior IC who happened to work at a famous company during its growth? Call two references and ask each the same blunt question: "Did revenue measurably move while they were accountable for it, and would you hire them again?" Push past the polite yes — ask what specifically moved, over what period, and what the operator personally did versus what the market gave them. A reference who can name the mechanism ("she rebuilt our discovery process and win rates went from 18 to 27 percent over two quarters") is describing an operator; a reference who offers only warmth ("great to work with, super sharp") is describing a personality. The RevOps hiring bar and the diligence questions are expanded at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/vetting-revenue-leaders.

## What should a fractional CRO cost, and how are engagements structured?

Do not anchor on a single number — the market is wide and depends on time commitment, stage, and whether equity is involved. That said, common structures cluster into three shapes. The most typical is a **monthly retainer** tied to a fixed number of days per week, which for an experienced fractional CRO commonly lands in the mid-four-figures to low-five-figures per month range depending on scope and market. The second is a **day-rate** or hourly arrangement for lighter-touch advisory. The third, increasingly common at venture-backed startups, layers a **small equity grant** (often a fraction of a percent, vesting over the engagement) on top of a reduced cash retainer, aligning the operator to the outcome rather than to billed hours.

Whatever the shape, the engagement must have an accountable scope, not an open-ended "advise us" mandate. Good fractional CRO engagements specify what the operator owns (the sales team, the forecast, the pipeline model, hiring the first two AEs), what success looks like in 90 days, and what stays with the founder. Ambiguity here is the number-one reason these arrangements fail: the founder expected an owner, the operator understood it as advice, and three months later revenue hasn't moved and nobody's clearly at fault.

It helps to think about what you are actually buying at each price point, because the retainer is not really priced by hours — it's priced by the seniority of judgment you're renting. A lower-cost, one-day-a-week arrangement typically buys you *direction*: the operator sets the strategy, designs the systems, and coaches your existing team to execute them. A higher-cost, three-day arrangement buys *presence*: the operator is in your pipeline reviews, your deal desk, and your hiring loops, actively driving rather than advising. Neither is better; they solve different problems. The failure mode is paying one-day money and expecting three-day presence — or paying for presence when what you needed was a sharp architect who could hand the blueprint to a capable internal team. Match the cadence to whether your gap is *design* or *drive*.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Define scope and owned outcomes] --> B[Agree retainer or day rate]
    B --> C[Optional equity for alignment]
    C --> D[30 day paid trial]
    D --> E{Revenue signals moving}
    E -->|Yes| F[Extend to ongoing engagement]
    E -->|No| G[End cleanly and reassess scope]
```

Always start with a **paid trial** — a scoped 30-day engagement with a concrete deliverable (a rebuilt forecast, a diagnosed pipeline, a hiring plan executed) — before committing to a rolling arrangement. It protects both sides: you see how they operate inside your actual mess, and they confirm the problem is one they can move. Founders who skip the trial and sign a six-month retainer on the strength of a good interview are the ones who write the cautionary posts. One more mechanical detail worth getting right up front: agree on the notice period and IP terms before the trial starts, not after. A clean fractional engagement is month-to-month with a 30-day notice on either side and clear language that anything the operator builds — playbooks, models, dashboards — belongs to the company. Lock that in early and the off-ramp stays clean if the fit isn't there. More on structuring the first engagement lives at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-engagement-structure.

## When is a fractional CRO the wrong hire?

Sourcing well doesn't help if the role is wrong for your stage. A fractional CRO fixes a *scaling* problem — you have proven that customers will pay, founder-led selling has generated repeatable deals, and now you need a professional to systematize and expand the motion. If you have **not** yet found product-market fit, a fractional CRO is premature; no comp plan or pipeline model conjures demand that isn't there, and you'll burn cash dressing up a motion that shouldn't scale yet. At that stage you need the founders to keep selling and learning directly.

The role is also wrong when what you actually need is a **full-time VP of Sales** to grind daily in the pipeline, or a hands-on **SDR/AE hire** to make calls. Fractional CROs architect and lead; they don't personally dial fifty prospects a day. If your gap is execution capacity rather than leadership and system design, you're hiring the wrong altitude. Conversely, if you're a Series B-plus company with a real revenue team that needs full-time daily leadership and board-facing ownership, a fractional CRO is likely too part-time — you've outgrown the model and should hire full-time.

There's a middle failure mode too: hiring a fractional CRO as a **crutch to avoid a hard decision**. If your real problem is a broken product, a wrong ICP, or a founder who won't let go of sales, a part-time revenue leader can't fix it in one or two days a week, and the engagement becomes an expensive way to postpone the reckoning. Be honest about whether the constraint is genuinely revenue *leadership* before you spend the search.

The founder-attachment version of this is the most common and the least discussed. Many early revenue problems are not really system problems — they're a founder who is still the best salesperson in the building and has not decided to let anyone else own the number. A fractional CRO cannot lead a motion the founder won't release; they end up shadow-boxing, making recommendations that get quietly overridden in the next deal call. Before you hire, ask yourself honestly: am I ready to let this person set quota, restructure comp, and tell me a deal I love isn't real? If the answer is no, fix that first, because the best operator in the market cannot out-work a founder who won't hand over the wheel. The stage-fit decision is mapped in more detail at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/when-to-hire-revenue-leader.

## How do I run the search so it actually closes?

Treat it like a compressed executive search, not a job posting. Start with a one-page **role brief**: the specific revenue problem, the motion (inbound PLG, outbound sales-led, channel, hybrid), the stage, the days-per-week you want, and the 90-day outcome that would make the hire obviously worth it. This document does double duty — it forces you to clarify what you actually need, and it lets referrers and marketplaces route you precise matches instead of generalists.

Run channels in parallel and give it two to four weeks. Send referral asks on day one (they have the longest latency and the highest quality), open a marketplace search the same day for volume, and reserve LinkedIn outreach for filling specific expertise gaps the first two channels miss. Aim to get **three to five genuinely qualified candidates** into first calls — fewer than three and you have no comparison; more than six and you're not filtering hard enough at the top of the funnel. Screen ruthlessly against the operator-vs-coach questions before you spend a founder's hour on a call.

Sequence the calls themselves deliberately. A good first call is 30 minutes and does exactly two things: pressure-tests the operator-vs-coach signal, and lets the candidate ask *you* sharp questions — because a real revenue leader interrogates your motion before they'll commit to owning it. A candidate who takes the brief at face value and doesn't probe your ICP, your win rates, or your churn is either not curious or not senior; either way it's a tell. Reserve the deeper 60-minute working session for your top two, and use it to co-diagnose a real problem live — hand them last quarter's pipeline and watch how they think. You learn more from thirty minutes of watching someone reason through your actual data than from an hour of them narrating their résumé.

Then converge fast. Take your top one or two into a **paid 30-day trial** with a real deliverable, check two references each in parallel, and make the extend/end decision on evidence — did the forecast get sharper, did pipeline discipline improve, did the first hire land — rather than on rapport. The founders who complain that fractional CROs "didn't work out" almost always skipped either the scoped trial or the reference calls. Do both and the model works as designed: senior revenue leadership at a fraction of the cost and commitment of a full-time CRO, with a clean off-ramp if the fit isn't there.

## Related questions
### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO *owns* an outcome — the forecast, the team, the number — part-time as an embedded leader. A consultant advises and hands off frameworks without carrying accountability for whether revenue actually moves.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?
Typically one to three days a week per client. Many carry two or three concurrent engagements, so confirm their total load to ensure they'll have real bandwidth for yours during crunch periods.

### Can a fractional CRO become full-time later?
Yes, and it's a common, healthy path. The fractional engagement functions as an extended mutual trial; if the fit is strong and the company scales into needing full-time leadership, converting a proven fractional CRO de-risks the permanent hire enormously.

### Do fractional CROs take equity?
Often, especially at venture-backed startups. A small equity grant (frequently under 1%, vesting over the engagement) layered on a reduced cash retainer aligns the operator to the revenue outcome rather than to billed hours.

### What stage company should hire a fractional CRO?
Usually post-product-market-fit companies from Seed to Series B, where founder-led selling has proven repeatable demand but the business can't yet justify a full-time CRO's base plus equity.

## FAQ
**How much does a fractional CRO cost per month?**
It varies widely by time commitment, stage, and whether equity is included. Retainers commonly sit in the mid-four-figures to low-five-figures per month for one to three days a week. Always tie the fee to a defined scope and days, never to open-ended availability.

**Where is the best place to find a fractional CRO?**
Start with warm referrals from your investors and founder peers — the highest-signal channel — then run a parallel search on fractional-executive marketplaces like Bolster, Go Fractional, Continuum, and Chief Outsiders for volume.

**How do I vet a fractional CRO?**
Confirm they've personally carried a quota or revenue P&L and hit it more than once at your stage and motion. Ask for a specific comp plan they designed, their pipeline-coverage rationale, and a 30-day plan — then call two references and ask if revenue measurably moved.

**Should I hire a fractional CRO or a full-time VP of Sales?**
Hire fractional when you need revenue *leadership and system design* part-time. Hire a full-time VP of Sales when you need someone in the pipeline daily executing and managing reps hands-on. They solve different problems at different altitudes.

**How long do fractional CRO engagements last?**
Most run three to twelve months, often starting with a scoped 30-day paid trial. Some convert to full-time; others end cleanly once the revenue motion is systematized and can be handed to an internal leader.

**What's a red flag when hiring a fractional CRO?**
The biggest is someone who talks only in frameworks and principles rather than specific numbers — ramp times, attainment percentages, comp mechanics. Other red flags: no carried-quota history, vague scope, resistance to a paid trial, and references who won't say revenue moved.

**Can a fractional CRO help before product-market fit?**
Generally no. A fractional CRO scales a proven motion; they can't manufacture demand that doesn't exist yet. Pre-PMF, founders should keep selling directly and learning from the market before hiring revenue leadership.

**Do fractional CROs work with multiple companies at once?**
Yes — most serve two to four clients concurrently, which is how the model stays affordable. Ask about their current load and how they protect bandwidth for each client during high-intensity stretches like a re-forecast or a key hire.

**How do I write a role brief for a fractional CRO search?**
Keep it to one page: the specific revenue problem, your motion and stage, the days per week you want, and the single 90-day outcome that would make the hire obviously worth it. A precise brief lets referrers and marketplaces route exact matches instead of generalists.
